rmk:
Cet enregistrement a été réalisé en milieu naturel , sur une place de rendez-vous que nous avions repéré lors d'enquêtes naturalistes avec le PNR du Verdon. Pendant plusieurs soirs la meute chantait plus ou moins aux mêmes horaires. Le 30 septembre 2023 nous avons tenté notre chance sans vraiment y croire. A notre grande surprise, le chant à débuté alors que nous n'étions pas encore prêt pour l'enregistrement. Nous avons manqué environ une minute de chant.


Les enregistrements ont été réalisé avec un système parabolique "fait maison", composé d'un plat wildtronic , couplé avec 4 capsules aom 5024 et un Tascam dr05x

Quelques modifications mineures ont été apportées sur cet enregistrement: 

-suppression ou nettoyage de bruits de manipulations. 
- amplification de 3db des premières secondes pour équilibrer le gain de la bande son.

House mouse (*Mus musculus*): A House mouse eats banana in a kitchen. 
This is my "retaliation" to a House mouse who chose to move in with us in winter 2023/24. Since then, it resides in the kitchen and eluded successfully the life-traps I have put up to repatriate it to nature. A very clever and discrete mouse indeed! I assume it is a female, as it doesn't smell like mouse in the kitchen, but I can't say for sure, though I have seen it on a few occasions. As it causes not much mayhem, we let it live with us. But, I wanted it to be documented, so I put up the recorder extremely close to a banana, as the mouse loves to eat banana (or other fruit as well). 

I wasn't sure if the recorder would capture the usually high frequencies of mouse calls, I was rather surprised that it did register frequencies up to 40 kHz! Don't expect too much of it, the sensitivity in these extreme frequency bands is low, and I would not expect it to register calls of bats or other animals, If you don't get real close to them. It worked out only because of the close distance (say three to five centimeters) to the mouse and some thoughtful editing (see below), and thus you can hear it munching, and there are some faint eeks and whistles towards the end of the clip. They can be heard much better in the modified version of the recording. However, I suggest using good headphones to hear them, and please listen closely. The sounds are there. I will have another go with another set-up including a better recorder with a much more sensitive microphone connected to it.

This is a version of XC999552 lowered by three octaves (87.5%). The speed, however, has not been changed, so the duration is the same as the in the original file. The calling and eeking should be heard easier in the lower register, now.

The expertise of Stuart Newson about this particular recording:

"I don’t think that these were produced by a Sorex species, as you note, the calls are too slow. I also considered Nyctalus noctula social calls (trills) briefly, but haven given this some thought, I don’t think that these were produced by Nyctalus noctula either.

I also considered the ‘mouse’ call of Cyanistes caeruleus – these calls are like slowed down shrew calls like these, but having a check, the calls here are too high in frequency for this species to be possible.

That brings me on to what I think is the most likely possibility, that these were produced by a Crocidura species. In the Netherlands, I have done a lot of work on the sound identification Crocidura russula, but it very rarely produces pronounced trills in its calls – I don’t think that I can completely exclude this possibility, but I would be surprised if they were produced by this species.

This leaves me with Crocidura leucodon. This is the only shrew species in the Netherlands I think, where I have only seen a small number of recordings and I don’t understand its vocalisations.

I think in summary I think that the calls here were most likely to have been produced by a Crocidura species – perhaps Crocidura russula, but it would be good to know if C. leucodon is present in your part of the country to see if this species is possible."

"I discussed and showed these recordings with a colleague of mine Simon Gillings today, which further confirmed my thinking that the calls here couldn't have been produced by a bird species."
